title: Recognize the form
prompt: "Find the minimum ship capacity that delivers all packages within D days." Why does binary-search-on-answer apply?
options: Feasibility is monotonic: if capacity c works, every capacity > c also works — so the answer space splits cleanly
explanation: Monotonic feasibility (fail...fail, work...work) means binary search finds the boundary. You write a `canShip(capacity)` simulator and search capacities.

title: Drill: lower bound
prompt: From memory: return the index of the FIRST element ≥ `target` in sorted `nums` (or `nums.length` if none). This is form 2 on indices: `lo = 0, hi = nums.length`, feasible(mid) = `nums[mid] >= target`.

solution.explanation: The workhorse variant: it handles duplicates, missing targets, and insert positions in one shape. Java's Arrays.binarySearch does NOT give you this cleanly.

hints: The condition `nums[mid] >= target` is false for a prefix and true for the rest. What are you looking for in that sequence?
Search for the first true: keep mid when it satisfies the condition, otherwise jump past it. `hi` starts at `nums.length` ("none qualify").
Feasible → `hi = mid`; infeasible → `lo = mid + 1`; loop `while (lo < hi)`, return `lo`.

title: Drill: integer square root (search on answer)
prompt: From memory (binary search on the answer): return floor(sqrt(x)) for x >= 0, without Math.sqrt. Search the answer space 1..x/2; feasibility is `mid*mid <= x` (use long to avoid overflow).

solution.explanation: The predicate `mid * mid <= x` is monotonic (true, ..., true, false, ...), so binary search finds the last true. Using long avoids overflow near Integer.MAX_VALUE. O(log x) time, O(1) space.

hints: As a candidate answer grows, "candidate² ≤ x" goes from true to false exactly once.
Binary search candidates, remembering the largest one whose square still fits.
Cast before squaring: `(long) mid * mid <= x`, then `ans = mid; lo = mid + 1;`.

title: Template recall: search on the answer
prompt: From memory: Koko Eating Bananas — the smallest speed whose hours fit in `h`.
explanation: Feasible speeds form a suffix (no, no, yes, yes). A feasible `mid` might be the answer, so keep it with `hi = mid`; an infeasible one is discarded with `lo = mid + 1`. With `lo < hi` the range shrinks every step and ends with `lo == hi` = the first feasible speed.

title: Rotated array: which half?
prompt: Search `target = 6` in `nums = [6, 7, 0, 1, 2, 4, 5]`. Now `l = 0`, `r = 6`, `mid = 3` (`nums[mid] = 1`). What is the correct next step?
options: Right half is sorted (`nums[l]=6 > nums[mid]=1`); 6 is not in `[1..5]`, so `r = mid - 1`
Left half is sorted; 6 is in it, so `r = mid - 1`
Neither half is sorted, so scan linearly
explanation: Since `nums[l] > nums[mid]`, the rotation point is in the left half and the right half `[1,2,4,5]` is sorted. A range check is only trustworthy on the sorted half: 6 is outside `[1..5]`, so it must be on the left. Plain `nums[mid] < target → l = mid + 1` would skip the answer at index 0.

title: Drill: last index with value <= target
prompt: From memory: return the LAST index `i` with `nums[i] <= target` in sorted `nums`, or -1 if none. This is the "latest timestamp at or before t" lookup from Time Based Key-Value Store.

solution.explanation: `nums[i] <= target` is true for a prefix of a sorted array; we want the end of that prefix. Every qualifying mid is recorded and the search continues right, so `ans` ends as the last qualifying index. O(log n) time, O(1) space.

hints: In a sorted array, which indices satisfy `nums[i] <= target` — a prefix, a suffix, or scattered?
Binary search that prefix: when mid qualifies, remember it and look further right; otherwise look left.
`if (nums[mid] <= target) { ans = mid; l = mid + 1; } else r = mid - 1;` starting with `ans = -1`.
